mean: the last time or date by which a job must be finished
ex: The GST filing deadline is the 20th, so Meenakshi's accounts team in Chennai is working through the weekend.
ex2: The college fee deadline was Friday, so Baba stood in the bank queue in Bhopal from nine in the morning.
note: You 'meet' a deadline, not 'achieve' or 'complete' it. To ask for more time, request 'an extension'.

mean: the thing that matters most and must be dealt with first
ex: With the monsoon two weeks away, the panchayat's first priority is clearing the village drains.
ex2: For Anjali, a mother of two in Thane, a full night's sleep has quietly become a bigger priority than weekend parties.
note: If everything is 'top priority', nothing is. The verb is 'prioritise' (British spelling): 'prioritise the client's bug over the new feature'.

mean: having the duty to deal with something, and the blame if it fails
ex: Arjun is responsible for vendor payments, so ask him why the wedding caterer still hasn't been paid.
ex2: At the Ranji match, the twelfth man was responsible for carrying drinks and spare gloves out to the batters.
note: Responsible FOR a task, responsible TO a person (your manager). Not 'responsible of'.

mean: comments on someone's work about what is good and what to improve
ex: After her first client demo at the Pune office, Sneha asked her manager for honest feedback on the slides.
ex2: The chai stall owner near Dadar station asks his regulars for feedback whenever he tries a new masala mix.
note: Uncountable: 'some feedback' or 'a piece of feedback', never 'a feedback' or 'feedbacks', a very common Indian office error.

mean: to plan and arrange something so that it happens smoothly
ex: Farhan offered to organise the hostel farewell, from booking the hall to ordering forty plates of biryani.
ex2: Every Durga Puja, the residents of our Kolkata para organise a blood donation camp beside the pandal.
note: British and Indian spelling is 'organise'; American is 'organize'. Either is fine, but stay consistent within one document.

mean: to give part of your work or power to someone else to do
ex: As the new branch head in Lucknow, Kavya had to learn to delegate instead of checking every loan file herself.
ex2: At home, Amma has finally learnt to delegate: the children now buy the vegetables and Appa washes the dishes.
note: The verb is DEL-i-gayt; the noun (a person sent to a conference) is DEL-i-gut. You can delegate a task, but not the final blame.

mean: the ability to act on your own without being told; also a new plan
ex: Nobody asked Priya to fix the messy shared drive; she took the initiative and sorted every folder by client.
ex2: When the village handpump broke, a Class 10 girl took the initiative and wrote to the block office herself.
note: Two meanings: a quality ('she shows initiative') and a programme ('a new safety initiative'). Spelling has four i's: i-ni-ti-a-tive.

mean: expected to explain your actions and accept the results, good or bad
ex: The housing society committee is accountable to residents, so it must show exactly where the maintenance money went.
ex2: Fans want the selectors to be accountable for picking an unfit fast bowler for the World Cup squad.
note: Responsible = it is your job to do. Accountable = you must answer for the result. Many can be responsible; one person should be accountable.

mean: general agreement among most of the people in a group
ex: After two hours of argument at the Kolkata adda, the only consensus was that the tea had gone cold.
ex2: The family WhatsApp group finally reached a consensus: Nani's eightieth birthday will be celebrated in Shimla.
note: Spelt 'consensus', not 'concensus'. 'General consensus' repeats itself; 'consensus' alone is enough.

mean: possible to actually do, given the time, money and people you have
ex: Is it really feasible to launch the app before Diwali with only three developers?
ex2: With only one weekend free, a road trip from Delhi to Ladakh just isn't feasible.
note: Feasible means practical, not just 'possible'. A plan can be possible in theory but not feasible on your budget.

mean: to work with other people on a shared task
ex: Two Bengaluru startups agreed to collaborate on a Kannada voice assistant for farmers.
ex2: For the school science fair, Ishaan and Zoya decided to collaborate on a model of rainwater harvesting.
note: Collaborate WITH a person ON a project. 'Collaborate together' repeats itself; drop 'together'.

mean: to discuss with someone until you reach an agreement both can accept
ex: Before joining, Ankit tried to negotiate a higher salary and one work-from-home day each week.
ex2: At Sarojini Nagar market, Tanvi can negotiate a five-hundred-rupee kurta down to two hundred.
note: Usually said with 'sh': ni-GOH-shee-ayt ('see' is also heard in Britain). The noun is 'negotiation'.

mean: to make something bad less serious or less harmful
ex: Mumbai's civic body desilts the nullahs before June to mitigate flooding during the heaviest rain.
ex2: Farmers in Vidarbha use drip irrigation to mitigate the damage when the monsoon arrives late.
note: You mitigate a problem directly, never 'mitigate against' it. Don't confuse with 'militate against' (to work against).

mean: the freedom to make your own decisions without being controlled
ex: The startup gives each team the autonomy to choose its own tools, as long as it hits its quarterly targets.
ex2: After moving into a PG in Pune, Riya enjoyed the autonomy of choosing her own meals and hours.
note: Adjective: autonomous ('an autonomous college'). Autonomy still comes with accountability: you are free to decide, and you answer for the result.

mean: helpful and meant to improve something, not just to find fault
ex: Instead of just calling the report weak, Leela gave constructive suggestions for each section.
ex2: The coach's talk after the loss was constructive: he showed each bowler one mistake on video and one fix.
note: 'Constructive criticism' says what to fix and how. Its opposite is 'destructive': criticism that only hurts.

mean: one slow point that holds up the whole process
ex: The single baggage scanner at the metro gate became a bottleneck during the morning rush.
ex2: In Patna, the old narrow bridge over the canal is a bottleneck that jams traffic every evening.
note: Like the narrow neck of a bottle. Often a person: if every approval waits for one boss, that boss is the bottleneck.

mean: to repeat a process again and again, improving it each time
ex: The design team will iterate on the payment screen after watching how kirana owners in Indore actually use it.
ex2: Nani kept trying to iterate on her mango pickle recipe, changing the salt or mustard a little each summer.
note: A startup and software word. Don't confuse with 'reiterate' (to say again). Noun: 'the third iteration of the design'.

mean: the official power or order given to someone to do a particular job
ex: The committee's mandate is only to suggest a new canteen menu, not to change the office timings.
ex2: The RBI's mandate is to keep inflation within a set range, not to decide how the government spends.
note: Also a verb: 'the rule mandates helmets for both riders'. After an election, the winner's authority from voters is called a 'mandate'.

mean: able to grow much bigger without breaking or costing much more
ex: Her tiffin service works for fifty homes, but is it scalable to five thousand across Hyderabad?
ex2: The reading programme worked in ten Rajasthan villages; now donors want to know if it is scalable across the state.
note: Scalable doesn't just mean 'big'; it means growth without costs growing as fast. The verb is 'scale up'.

mean: anyone affected by a decision or interested in its result
ex: Before redrawing the bus routes, the city consulted every stakeholder: drivers, shopkeepers, schoolchildren and daily commuters.
ex2: In a joint family, every cousin feels like a stakeholder when the old ancestral house is up for sale.
note: Wider than 'shareholder', who owns shares. Customers, staff and neighbours of a factory are all stakeholders.

mean: something, often a reward, that encourages you to do something
ex: The dairy cooperative gives farmers an incentive of two rupees extra per litre for cleaner milk.
ex2: Mrs Bose gives her son an incentive to read: one comic book for every novel he finishes.
note: An incentive pulls you towards an action; a 'disincentive' pushes you away. 'Motive' is your own inner reason; an incentive comes from outside.

mean: giving up some of one thing to get more of another
ex: The Gurugram job paid more, but the trade-off was a two-hour commute every day.
ex2: Choosing the cheaper flat in Bengaluru was a trade-off: more money saved, but no lift and no power backup.
note: The noun is hyphenated (a trade-off); the verb is two words: 'trade off speed against cost'.

mean: the ability to see what may happen and plan for it
ex: Thanks to her father's foresight, the family had savings ready when the shop shut during the lockdown.
ex2: The selectors showed foresight by giving young pacers matches long before the senior bowlers retired.
note: Opposite of 'hindsight', which is wisdom after the event. You show foresight before; you say 'in hindsight' after.

mean: able to make choices quickly and firmly; or settling a result clearly
ex: When the site crashed during the sale, Imran was decisive: he rolled back the update within minutes.
ex2: In the final over, the captain's decisive call to bring on the spinner won the match.
note: Don't confuse with 'divisive' (causing people to disagree). A 'decisive win' is a clear one, not a narrow one.

mean: when a group agrees too easily and nobody questions a bad idea
ex: The board fell into groupthink; nobody questioned the expansion plan until the losses began.
ex2: In our hostel, groupthink decided we would all skip the lecture; only Deepak asked whether attendance mattered.
note: Not the same as consensus. Consensus is real agreement after debate; groupthink is agreement because nobody dares to disagree.

mean: money or effort already spent that you can never get back
ex: The half-built godown is a sunk cost; spending more on a bad location will only lose more money.
ex2: The ticket money is a sunk cost, Ravi, so leave the boring film at the interval and come for chai.
with: treat it as a sunk cost
note: The 'sunk cost fallacy' is carrying on with something bad only because you've already invested in it, like sitting through a terrible film because you paid.

mean: a result or number you are trying to reach
ex: The sales team in Indore must hit a target of two hundred new accounts before March.
ex2: Kiran set herself a target of ten thousand steps a day on her walks along Marine Drive.
note: You 'meet', 'hit' or 'achieve' a target. As a verb it means aim at: 'ads that target teenagers'.

mean: a plan of how much money can be spent, and on what
ex: The project is already over budget, so the Chennai office has stopped all travel until April.
ex2: Our wedding budget had no room for a drone camera, but Chachu still booked one.
note: 'Over budget' means spending more than planned; 'on a tight budget' means with little money. Say BUJ-it, not 'bud-JET'.

mean: to give someone a job or task to do
ex: The manager will assign each new joiner a buddy for their first week in the Hyderabad office.
ex2: Our maths teacher likes to assign twenty sums every Friday, which ruins the whole weekend.
note: The g is silent: uh-SYNE. The noun 'assignment' means a task or a piece of homework.

mean: to organise people or things so they work well together
ex: Shalini's job is to coordinate between the Pune developers and the client in London.
ex2: The three sisters had to coordinate over the phone to decide who would bring which dish for Eid.
note: Coordinate WITH someone. The noun is common in complaints: 'poor coordination between departments'.

mean: an important stage reached in a project or in life
ex: Launching the app in Tamil and Marathi was a big milestone for the Bengaluru startup.
ex2: For Dadi, her grandson's first day at school was a milestone worth a box of laddoos for the whole street.
note: Literally the stones beside highways that mark distance. In project plans, milestones are the checkpoints.

mean: to watch over work and make sure it is done properly
ex: A senior engineer will oversee the building of the new flyover at Silk Board junction.
ex2: Every Diwali, Nanaji likes to oversee the rangoli, telling the grandchildren which colour goes where.
note: Don't confuse with 'overlook', which means to miss or ignore something. Past forms: oversaw, overseen.

mean: doing a job well without wasting time, money or effort
ex: The new billing software is so efficient that the clinic's morning queue is half as long.
ex2: Mumbai's dabbawalas run one of the most efficient delivery systems in the world, with very few mistakes.
note: Efficient = no waste; effective = it works. A meeting can be efficient (short) but not effective (nothing decided).

mean: to make a process simpler and faster by removing needless steps
ex: The passport office wants to streamline renewals so that people don't need three visits.
ex2: Ammi decided to streamline the morning rush by packing every tiffin the night before.
note: Common in office emails. Don't stop at the word; say which steps you actually removed.

mean: to decide how much of something each person or job gets
ex: The panchayat must allocate the new funds between the school roof and the village road.
ex2: The hostel warden will allocate rooms by lottery, so nobody can complain about favourites.
note: The noun is 'allocation'. 'Allot' is close and very common in India: 'allotted seats', 'allotted flats'.

mean: acting early to stop a problem, instead of waiting for it
ex: Instead of waiting for complaints, Nikhil was proactive and called every client after the server crash.
ex2: Be proactive about your health, Papa: get the blood test done before the doctor has to ask.
note: The opposite is 'reactive': responding only after something has gone wrong.

mean: how confident and keen a group feels about its work
ex: After three rounds of layoffs, morale in the Gurugram office was at an all-time low.
ex2: One early wicket lifted the team's morale, and soon every fielder was diving for the ball.
note: Morale (muh-RAHL) is spirit; moral (MOR-ul) is about right and wrong. 'Boost morale', never 'boost moral'.

mean: a possible future problem, or a plan kept ready for it
ex: The event company had a contingency plan: if the monsoon hit, the sangeet would move into the banquet hall.
ex2: Keep some money aside for every contingency, beta; hostel life in a new city always brings surprises.
note: Most often heard as 'contingency plan' (a Plan B) or 'contingency fund' (money kept aside for surprises).

mean: to lead a big effort or campaign from the front
ex: Dr Fernandes will spearhead the hospital's drive to cut waiting times in the emergency ward.
ex2: Two Class 12 students in Shillong decided to spearhead a clean-up of the lake after the festival.
note: Use it for big, bold efforts. For small jobs 'lead' is enough; 'spearhead a meeting' sounds odd.

mean: to control every small detail of other people's work, too closely
ex: Good managers set the goal and step back; they don't micromanage the font on every slide.
ex2: My uncle tends to micromanage every family trip, down to which dhaba we stop at for lunch.
note: Always negative. Such a person is a 'micromanager'. Trusting people with the result is the opposite.

mean: letting people do as they like, with very little control or guidance
ex: Her laissez-faire style works with senior engineers but leaves new interns completely lost.
ex2: The hostel warden was so laissez-faire that students played carrom in the corridor until two in the morning.
note: French for 'let do'. In economics it means the government staying out of business. Keep the hyphen.

mean: the idea that work grows to fill all the time you give it
ex: Give the team a month for a two-day task and Parkinson's law kicks in: it will take the whole month.
ex2: With the whole Sunday free, Parkinson's law took over, and cleaning one cupboard somehow filled the entire day.
note: Named after the writer C. Northcote Parkinson (1955). The cure is a short, firm deadline.
